lines.text: אגן 12 אדר
אַגָּן m. pr. a trough for washing gar-
ments, λουτήρ, from root אָגַן q. v. then
any laver, basin, bowl; constr. אַגַּן Cant.
—Arab. and Syr. إِجَّانَة, ܐܰܓܳܢܳܐ, id.
אֲגַפִּים m. plur. (r. גָּפַף) a word found
only in Ezekiel, hosts, armies, Ez. 12, 14.
17, 21. 38, 6. 9. 39, 4. It corresponds to
the Chald. אֲגַף, גַּף, wing; hence pr.
wings of an army, comp. כְּנָפַיִם Is. 8, 8.
The Arabic and Chaldee have the same
trop. use of the word wings; comp.
Comment. on Is. l. c.
* אָגַר fut. יֶאֱגֹר 1. to gather, to col-
lect, e. g. the harvest, Deut. 28, 39. Prov.
6, 8. 10, 5. Comp. גּוּר no. 3, and יָגַר;
also Gr. ἀγείρω. The primary idea seems
to be that of scraping together, comp.
גָּרַר. By softening the letter ר we have
אָגַל and גָּלַל, which denote the rolling
and flowing together of water.
2. In the kindred dialects it has the
signif. to gain, to make profit, from the
idea of scraping together; and hence to
hire for wages; see אִגֶּרֶת.
Deriv. אִגֶּרֶת, אֲגוֹרָה, pr. n. אָגוּר, and
according to most אֲגַרְטָל.
אִגְּרָא Chald. stat. emphat. אִגַּרְתָּא, a
letter, epistle, i. q. Heb. אִגֶּרֶת q. v. Ezra
אֶגְרוֹף m. (for גְּרוֹף, Aleph. prosthet.
from r. גָּרַף no. 2) the fist, Ex. 21, 18. Is.
58, 4. So Sept. and Vulg. in both pas-
sages; the Rabbins also use this word
in the same sense.
אֲגַרְטָל m. Ezra 1, 9 אֲגַרְטְלֵי זָהָב, כֶּסֶף
Sept. Vulg. Syr. basins, chargers of gold,
of silver. In the Jerus. Talmud this
word is said to be compounded from אֲגַר
to collect, and טָלֶה a lamb, and basins
are so called, because the blood of lambs
is collected in them. But there is here
no mention of blood. It seems rather a
quadriliteral formed with א prosthet. and
denoting slaughter-basin, for גַּרְטֵל, גַּטֵּל,
see under letter ר; and this is prob. i. q.
קַטֵּל, קַטֵּל, (comp. Zab. גטל for קטל,)
from ܢܰܟܳܣ to slaughter, قَطَلَ to cut the
throat.—Some also hold it to be i. q. Gr.
κάρταλος, κάρταλλος, which in the Sept.
signifies a basket, fruit-basket, whence
Arab. قِرْطَلَّةٌ, Rabb. קַרְטִיל, Syr.
ܩܰܪܛܳܠܳܐ; and it might perhaps in Ezra
l. c. be understood of baskets of the first-
fruits. But this Greek word itself seems
rather of Semitic origin, from the verb
גָּדַל to plait.
אִגֶּרֶת f. plur. אִגְּרוֹת, a word of the
later Hebrew, a letter, epistle, espec.
spoken of royal letters and edicts, writ-
ten by public authority and transmitted
by a public courier, ἄγγαρος, to those to
whom they were directed, 2 Chr. 30, 1.
The word comes most prob. from an
obsol. form אַגָּר, which denoted one
hired, spec. a letter-carrier, courier, from
r. אָגַר no. 2; and was adopted by the
Greeks under the form ἄγγαρος, see
17, 19. Esth. 9, 26. 29.—Lorsbach, in
Stäudlin’s Beytr. V. p. 20, supposes it to
be derived from the Persian; comp. mod.
Pers. انڭاريدن engârîden, to paint, to
write, whence انڭاره engâreh, any writ-
ing.
אֵד m. vapour, mist, rising from the
earth and forming clouds, so called be-
cause it surrounds the earth like a veil
or covering, from r. אוּד no. 1. This
etymology is also supported by the Ara-
bic, in which إِيَادٌ (from r. آدَ mid. Ye,
to surround, comp. in אוּד no. 1) is any
Hiph. causat. inf. לַאֲדִיב for לְהַאֲדִיב
thing which protects and strengthens,
as a bulwark, bark, a veil, also the atmo-
sphere. Corresponding is also Chald.
אֵיד vapour.—Gen. 2, 6. Job 36, 27.
אֹדוֹת see אוֹדוֹת.
* אָדַב by transpos. i. q. דָּאַב q. v. to
pine away, to languish. Found only in
1 Sam. 2, 33. Comp. espec. Deut. 28,
אַדְבְּאֵל (perh. miracle of God, from
أَدْبٌ miracle) Adbeel, pr. n. of a son of
Ishmael, Gen. 25, 13.
* אֲדַד obsol. root, Arab. أَدَّ i. q. هَدَّ
to befall any one, as misfortune; whence
أَدٌّ misfortune. Hence אֲדוֹ and
אֲדַד Adad, pr. n. of an Edomite, 1 K.
11, 17; called also הֲדַד Hadad, v. 14.

line_status.note: Under the dageshed gimel the print shows a three-dot segol (אִגֶּרֶת), not a sheva; Reading B's אִגְּרֶת is wrong.
Under the aleph of the final word the print shows a ḥaṭef pataḥ (short stroke plus two shewa dots), matching the aleph of the headword אֲגַרְטָל above, not a qameṣ; Reading B is correct.
Both tets in the two leading words carry a visible dagesh dot in the print; Reading B drops the dagesh from the second קַטֵּל. Zabian forms גטל and קטל are unpointed, as both readings have them.
Arabic middle letter has the loop + tall ascender of ṭāʾ (قَطَلَ), not tāʾ; Syriac word is nun–kaph–samekh ܢܟܣ (pthaha on nun, zqapha on kaph), not ܩܛܠ. Reading B matches.

A small damma-shaped mark is clearly printed above the final ة (tanwīn ḍamm, ‑ةٌ), so Reading B is correct; the Hebrew קַרְטִיל (plene yod, no dagesh) and the order Arab./Rabb./Syr. match both readings.

Under the aleph the print shows a flat patach, not a hiriq dot; under the gimel (which carries a dagesh) there is a qamets (horizontal stroke with a descending tick), not a patach. Compare line 3's אָגַר, where the vowels are reversed — line 1 is clearly אַגָּר, Reading B.
Final letter of both Arabic words is dāl (د) with no dot above, not nūn (ن); consistent with r. אוּד and "to surround". Reading B is correct.
Under the aleph the print shows two vertical dots plus a short stroke — ḥaṭef‑pataḥ (אֲ), not a plain qamets as in A. The rest (Arabic أَدَّ i. q. هَدَّ) matches both readings.

The mark above the hamza on the alif is a short slanted stroke (fatha), identical in shape to the vowel on the verb أَدَّ in line 1 — not the curled loop of a damma. Dal carries shadda + tanwin damma; the Hebrew אֲדוֹ with hateph-pathach and plene vav is as both readings have it.
